intros.market: The WebPKI remains highly concentrated with five CAs controlling 91.6% of all issuance. Internet Security Research Group leads at 38.5%, followed by Google Trust Services at 20.7% and DigiCert at 14.7%. The CR3 concentration ratio of 73.9% means three organizations control nearly three-quarters of the ecosystem, while 75 tail CAs share the remaining 8.4% of issuance among 89 total trusted authorities.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs and only 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating the largest source of store disagreement. This fragmentation forces CAs to maintain multiple certification paths and creates operational complexity where a certificate chain valid in Edge may fail validation in Chrome or Safari.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 2307 indicates high concentration just below formal oligopoly thresholds, with systemic dependency risks concentrated in the top three providers. If any of the top two CAs experienced a distrust event, between 20% and 39% of the web would face immediate certificate failures. This concentration amplifies the blast radius of any single CA failure while creating barriers to entry that reinforce the existing market structure seen in the 75-provider long tail.
intros.tail: 75 CAs operate in the long tail with minimal issuance share but full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for the ecosystem. These providers collectively represent less than 9% of certificates but maintain the same universal trust privileges as high-volume operators. Low issuance volumes may correlate with less operational maturity and fewer resources for compliance infrastructure, yet their roots carry equal weight in browser trust decisions.
intros.geo: US-based CAs account for 91.6% of all issuance despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted authorities, while 44 European CAs produce just 8.4% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs contribute 0.08%. This geographic concentration creates systemic dependency on US jurisdiction and operational practices. The stark imbalance between CA count and issuance share reveals that most non-US CAs operate in the long tail with minimal market presence despite achieving trust store inclusion.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but account for only 0.07% of issuance, operating almost entirely in the long tail. These entities introduce sovereign control points into the WebPKI trust fabric, carrying different operational incentives than commercial providers. Their presence intersects with jurisdiction risk considerations, particularly for the five high-risk countries identified where state CAs could face compelled disclosure or surveillance obligations.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance obligations: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk profiles. CAs incorporated in these jurisdictions face potential legal frameworks that could compel certificate issuance, key disclosure, or surveillance cooperation regardless of operational practices. These legal risks layer onto the geographic concentration showing 91.6% US issuance and the 30 government-operated CAs in the trust stores.
intros.ops: 1,550 incidents have been recorded across 54 CAs, with misissuance leading at 604 cases followed by governance failures at 495 and revocation problems at 328. Only 26% of incidents are self-detected while 18% come from external researchers and 17% from automated tools, revealing significant gaps in internal controls. Root program oversight catches just 4% of incidents directly, and audits detect only 8%, pointing to systematic surveillance failures that surface later in distrust patterns and governance coverage rates.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture reflects ongoing migration from legacy algorithms to modern standards, though specific algorithm and key size distributions require examination of current root inventories. Standards compliance intersects with the regulatory surface that has grown to 6,664 obligations, a 121x increase since 2000. The crypto modernization challenge compounds with BR readiness requirements as CAs must simultaneously manage algorithm transitions and prepare for certificate validity reductions.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the ecosystem with 14 attributed to compliance and operations failures rather than technical cryptographic breaks. Negligent noncompliance accounts for 7 cases, willful circumvention for 3, and demonstrated incompetence for 3, revealing patterns where operational failures rather than malice drive distrust. The median runway of 1,185 days from incident detection to distrust reflects both root program patience and the complexity of unwinding trust relationships, though 10 events show patterns of repeated issues rather than isolated failures.
intros.policy: Of 43 active TLS CAs measured against SC-081 validity thresholds, 4 remain at risk at the 200-day limit, 5 at risk at 100 days, and only 8 ready for the 47-day requirement with a median usage of 67 days. This readiness challenge unfolds against a compliance surface that has grown from 55 obligations in 2000 to 6,664 today, a 121x increase with 5,056 now mandatory. Zero ballots have passed since 2022 to modernize the baseline requirements even as CAs navigate 76% mandatory obligation density, creating a static rulebook for a dynamic threat landscape.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% Chrome and 78.0% Mozilla participation in 2019 incidents to just 18.4% Chrome and 9.9% Mozilla in 2025, with Apple at 5.4% and Microsoft at 0.0%. Chrome has commented substantively on 293 of 730 oversight bugs while Mozilla shows 249 of 818, but recent substantive engagement has dropped sharply to 112 and 47 respectively. This declining oversight directly correlates with the 26% self-detection rate and explains why audits catch only 8% of incidents, leaving 18% to external researchers who fill the surveillance gap.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 actively participate, leaving 35 with zero contribution to standards development. Sectigo leads organizational engagement while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually with 1 endorsement, demonstrating concentrated standards leadership. This participation gap means most CAs consuming the regulatory surface of 6,664 obligations contribute nothing to its evolution, creating a disconnect between those writing rules and those operating under them.
intros.audit: Audit letters show a 31% in-period detection rate, meaning auditors identified only 128 of 414 incidents that fell within their audit scope and timeframe. 38 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and Bugzilla incident histories, while 5 letters carry qualified opinions and 11 CAs changed auditors in 2025. Quality scores average 55 to 85 across top auditors while transparency gaps range from 73 to 100 days, revealing systematic surveillance failures where annual compliance theater coexists with operational reality captured in the 1,550 total incidents.
